anchor: draw the line where the violet tint ends and the orange tint begins
note: Melville compares the border between sanity and madness to the unmarked border between colors in a rainbow.

anchor: the exact line of demarkation
note: Demarkation: a boundary, a line marking a limit.

anchor: some professional experts will
note: Melville mocks expert witnesses in madness trials who give opinions for a fee.

anchor: any degree of aberration
note: Aberration: a departure from what is normal, here a mental lapse.

anchor: could not have happened at a worse juncture
note: Juncture: a particular point in time, a critical moment.

anchor: close on the heel of the suppressed insurrections
note: Insurrections: open revolts, here the mutinies of 1797.

anchor: two qualities not readily interfusable—prudence and rigour
note: Interfusable: able to be blended. Prudence and rigour pull in opposite directions.

anchor: In the jugglery of circumstances
note: Jugglery: a trick of shifting things around so they look different.

anchor: that martial code whereby it was formally to be judged
note: Martial code: the military law that governs sailors and soldiers.

anchor: constituted the most heinous of military crimes
note: Heinous: shockingly evil, a crime of the worst kind.

anchor: circumspectness not less than promptitude
note: Circumspectness: care in looking at every side before acting.

anchor: in the confidential talk of more than one or two gun-rooms and cabins
note: The gun-room was the junior officers’ mess; the cabins were the senior officers’ quarters.
source: W. H. Smyth, The Sailor’s Word-Book (1867), “Gun-room”, https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/26000

anchor: professional jealousy of Starry Vere
note: Professional jealousy: resentment among rivals in the same career.

anchor: Some imaginative ground for invidious comment
note: Invidious: likely to cause ill will. Some basis existed for hostile gossip.

anchor: fain would the Indomitable’s Captain have deferred
note: Fain: gladly. Deferred: put off to a later time.

anchor: a true military officer is in one particular like a true monk
note: Both give up personal will for a higher obedience.

anchor: Not with more of self-abnegation
note: Self-abnegation: denying oneself, putting aside personal wishes.

anchor: slumbering embers of the Nore
note: The Nore was the site of the second fleet mutiny of 1797. Vere fears it may spark again.

anchor: monopolizing to himself the perils of moral responsibility
note: Monopolizing: taking all of something for oneself.

anchor: a summary court of his own officers
note: Summary: done quickly without ordinary formalities.

anchor: the right of maintaining a supervision of it
note: Supervision: oversight, watching over a process.

anchor: formally or informally interposing at need
note: Interposing: stepping in between, intervening.

anchor: the First Lieutenant, the Captain of Marines, and the Sailing Master
note: The Sailing Master navigated the ship. The First Lieutenant was the captain’s deputy.
source: W. H. Smyth, The Sailor’s Word-Book (1867), “Master”, https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/26000

anchor: an officer of marines
note: Marines were sea soldiers who guarded the ship and fought in boarding actions.

anchor: a difficult case unprecedented in his prior experience
note: Unprecedented: never having happened before, with no earlier example.

anchor: latent misgiving
note: Latent: hidden. Misgiving: a feeling of doubt.

anchor: inclined to obesity
note: Obesity: being very fat, here the officer’s comfortable build.

anchor: a moral dilemma involving aught of the tragic
note: Dilemma: a choice between two hard options.

anchor: under the poopdeck
note: The poop deck is the raised deck at the stern of the ship.

anchor: a yet smaller compartment leaving a space between
note: The cabin had a small room on each side, one used as a jail and one as a dead-house.

anchor: the ship’s beam
note: Beam: the width of a ship at its widest part.

anchor: embrasures for short carronades
note: Embrasures: openings in a wall for guns. Carronades were short, light ship’s cannon.

anchor: Billy Budd was arraigned
note: Arraigned: called before the court to answer a charge.

anchor: deposing as to the manner
note: Deposing: giving sworn testimony before a court.

anchor: the last man they would have suspected
note: The three officers could not believe Billy had a mutinous plan.

anchor: taking judicial primacy
note: Primacy: first place, here as presiding officer.

anchor: I have eaten the King’s bread and I am true to the King
note: To eat the King’s bread is to serve and be fed by him, so owing loyalty.

anchor: an innate repugnance to playing a part
note: Innate: born with. Repugnance: strong dislike.

anchor: uninstructed honor
note: Uninstructed: untaught. Billy’s honor has not been trained by rules.

anchor: with the blind feeling now his, that nothing really was being hatched
note: Hatched: plotted. Billy feels no real plot exists.

anchor: Nevertheless he strove some way to answer
note: Strove: tried hard, made an effort.

anchor: the point you make is hardly material
note: Material: relevant, mattering to the matter at hand.

anchor: a martial court must needs in the present case confine its attention
note: Needs: must. A martial court judges only the deed.

anchor: a wistful interrogative look
note: Wistful: sadly longing. Interrogative: questioning.

anchor: some elucidation of a previous gesture ambiguous to the canine intelligence
note: Elucidation: making clear. Canine: of dogs.

anchor: a prejudgement on the speaker’s part
note: Prejudgement: a decision made before hearing all the evidence.

anchor: who might shed lateral light
note: Lateral: from the side. Indirect light on the case.

anchor: a matter for psychologic theologians to discuss
note: Vere says the question of why Claggart lied belongs to theologians, not to a military court.

anchor: the lasting tongue-tie of—him—in yonder
note: Tongue-tie: loss of speech. Claggart is dead and cannot speak.

anchor: scarce in equable tones
note: Equable: steady, even-tempered, not at all calm here.

anchor: in one of his absent fits
note: Vere often falls into dreamy fits of abstraction.

anchor: to-and-fro paced the cabin athwart
note: Athwart: across, from side to side of the ship.

anchor: inly deliberating how best to put them
note: Inly: inwardly. Deliberating: thinking carefully.

anchor: principles that were axioms to himself
note: Axioms: statements accepted as obviously true.

anchor: that imputation of a certain pedantry
note: Pedantry: fussy showing-off of learning.

anchor: your coadjutor
note: Coadjutor: an assistant or colleague.

anchor: a troubled hesitancy
note: Hesitancy: reluctance to act, holding back.

anchor: scruple vitalized by compassion
note: Scruple: a moral hesitation. Vitalized: given life.

anchor: tend to enervate decision
note: Enervate: to weaken, drain of energy.

anchor: Speculatively regarded, it well might be referred to a jury of casuists
note: Casuists are moral philosophers who work out the right answer in particular hard cases. Vere says a jury of casuists could argue it forever.

anchor: mindless of palliating circumstances
note: Palliating: making less severe. Mitigating.

anchor: the prisoner’s overt act
note: Overt: done openly, not hidden.

anchor: adjudge to summary and shameful death
note: Adjudge: to decide by judgment.

anchor: do these buttons that we wear attest that our allegiance is to Nature?
note: Naval uniform buttons carried the King’s mark. Vere says officers serve the King, not Nature.

anchor: this be the element where we move and have our being
note: Echoes Paul’s speech in Acts: “in him we live, and move, and have our being.” Vere applies it to the sea.
source: The Bible (King James Version), Acts 17:28, https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/10

anchor: Would it be so much we ourselves that would condemn as it would be martial law
note: Martial law is the suspension of ordinary law in war. It is the will of the commander, not law in the strict sense.

anchor: tender kinswoman of the accused
note: Kinswoman: a female relative who comes to plead.

anchor: that imperial one formulated in the code
note: Imperial: supreme. The code of military law outranks private conscience.

anchor: the Articles of War
note: The Articles of War were the written code of discipline for the army and navy. A blow struck at a superior was a capital crime.

anchor: At the Last Assizes it shall acquit
note: The Last Assizes is the Last Judgment before God. Assizes were court sessions held in English counties.
source: The Bible (King James Version), Revelation 20:12, https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/10

anchor: the law of the Mutiny Act
note: The Mutiny Act was the English law that made mutiny and disobedience in the army and navy punishable by military courts.

anchor: what reck we of it?
note: Reck: to care, to take heed.

anchor: in the same swath with our volunteers
note: Swath: a strip cut by a scythe. The enemy would mow down impressed and volunteer alike.

anchor: the regicidal French Directory
note: Regicidal: involved in killing a king. The French had executed Louis XVI in 1793.

anchor: convict and yet mitigate the penalty
note: Mitigate: to make less severe.

anchor: consider the consequences of such clemency
note: Clemency: mercy, leniency toward an offender.

anchor: a flagrant act of mutiny
note: Flagrant: glaringly obvious, impossible to overlook.

anchor: Your clement sentence they would account pusillanimous
note: Pusillanimous: cowardly, lacking courage, weak-spirited.

anchor: Loyal lieges, plain and practical
note: Lieges: loyal subjects of a lord or king.

anchor: without the faculty, hardly had the inclination, to gainsay
note: Gainsay: to deny or contradict.

anchor: the unconfirmed tone of the fleet at the time
note: Unconfirmed: not yet settled or firm.

anchor: a writer whom few know
note: Melville quotes himself, a writer known to few.

anchor: Little ween the snug card-players in the cabin
note: Ween: to think or imagine.

anchor: sentenced to be hung at the yard-arm in the early morning watch
note: The early morning watch was the hours before dawn. Hanging at the yard-arm was the navy’s way to execute mutineers.

anchor: without appeal
note: A drum-head court’s sentence could not be appealed.
